placements.story: A constant, quiet renewal, carried out entirely by volunteers. Rain lily clumps are lifted and divided where they have filled in, offsets are carried to a bed that has none, and people bring bulbs from their own gardens at home. Nothing about it is scheduled or budgeted — it happens a handful at a time, season after season, and the borders reach a little further into the park each year. The succulent garden and the shade garden are edged this way; more beds join the list every season. Randy, 2026-08-30: "somebody is spreading them around constantly and edging more areas, bringing more from home. Non stop building up." It is why any list of rain lily placements is a sample rather than an inventory — the planting is still being made.
placements.notes:
Rain lilies EDGE these beds rather than growing as a specimen — Randy 2026-08-30: "the first thing in a lot of planting islands... they line the succulent garden which has to be 50yd long. One sign wouldn't be good enough." Invisible most of the year and up within days of heavy rain, so a permanent sign would stand in front of bare mulch for eleven months. A sign is for permanent presence; this is an EVENT, and belongs in Right Now.
⚠ THIS LIST IS A SAMPLE AND WILL NEVER BE COMPLETE. Randy, same day: "somebody is spreading them around constantly and edging more areas, bringing more from home. Non stop building up." A volunteer is propagating them and edging new beds every season, so any count of rain lily placements is out of date the moment it is taken. Do not try to enumerate them, and do not treat missing edges as a gap in the data.

placements.story: Replacement fern for the one the park lost. Funded by park photographer Rhonda O while she was away for the summer; planting site chosen by Bev. Planted summer 2026.

placements.notes: Growing UP A PALM — almost certainly the Royal Palm at PLC-0103, 10.9 m away and the only palm within 29 m. Randy 2026-08-31: "They do have the Swiss cheese plant. 100% growing up a palm tree. It's massive." Observed once, by Lilah Thomas on 2026-06-24 (±8 m) — good accuracy for this corner of the park, where the median is nearer 24 m. NOT in the rare fruit grove: it carries the rare_fruit flag because the fruit is edible, and the MRFC list names it, but the plant itself is 60 m north in Pavilion Field among the staghorn ferns.

⚠ BELIEVED DEAD. The Rare Fruit Council's pineapple, on the pond edge behind the ramp up to the bathroom, ~10 m from the Pavilion Restroom Ramp. Randy, 2026-08-31: "It seems dead now. Was just an ordinary bromeliad looking thing but had gotten worse and worse." (A pineapple IS a bromeliad, and a declining one looks like any other — which is why it was easy to walk past.)
ONE observation ever: victoriashein, 2022-11-27, ±4 m. Nothing in the four years since. last_checked newer than last_seen records that it was looked for and not found.
KEPT ON PURPOSE, not deleted. The 2022 record is evidence it was once here, and this row is what explains its absence from the council's list next time somebody compares. The LIVING pineapple is PLC-0177, 86 m west in the succulent garden — a different plant, and fruiting.

DO NOT SHEAR — being trained as a shade tree. Terminalia buceras is a 40-50 ft shade tree; it is not sold or grown as a shrub, and whoever planted it here in open turf almost certainly intended shade. It is currently a sheared ball about 6-7 ft high and as wide, crowding a bench. PLAN: (1) mulch ring now, 3 in deep, 6-8 ft radius, kept off the trunk — the turf growing to the base is the main thing suppressing it; (2) stop all shearing, and flag the plant physically so mowers and volunteers can see it; (3) February, map the basal stems and choose ONE leader, then SUBORDINATE the competitors — shorten each by about a third back to a lateral at least 1/3 its diameter. Do not remove them at the base; that would strip the plant. Remove them gradually in years 3-4 once the leader dominates. Never more than 25% of live crown in a year, never top it. Roughly 8-12 years to a usable shade canopy. BENCH: consider moving it outside the future dripline — this species drops tannin-heavy fruit that stains permanently. NOT the same plant as PSBP-00467 Spiny Black Olive (Terminalia molinetii), which is correctly left as a dense shrub. Treating the two alike is how this one got sheared.

NOT YET RELOCATED — and Randy has already looked. Randy, 2026-09-01: "i was confident her observation was walters viburnum but I haven't found it yet... I figured I would eventually." The identification is not in doubt; the plant just has not been found on the ground. LOOK IN MID-FEBRUARY, NOT NOW. Viburnum obovatum is recorded in Florida 913 times in February and 68 times in June — thirteen to one. It is not commoner in February, it is FINDABLE in February: in bloom it is covered in white and unmissable, and out of bloom it is an anonymous small-leaved shrub in a mixed native bed. Bev's photo is dated 19 Mar 2025; every search since has happened in the eleven months when the plant does not announce itself. Coordinate from iNaturalist obs 266013464, +/-3 m, photographed by Bev Burdette (who has TWO observations in her life — she stopped for this one plant alone at 17:12 and recorded nothing else that day). Randy confirmed the area independently on 2026-09-01: "Yes butterfly garden area for sure." Nearest catalogued neighbours: PLC-0009 Firewheel (6 m), PLC-0103 Royal Palm (9 m), PLC-0097 Coontie Palm (10 m). ASK BEV FIRST — she may remember the bed, which collapses the whole problem. ON ARRIVAL: confirm leaves in OPPOSITE PAIRS, about an inch, spoon-shaped, and NO spines; set last_checked; take the second, third and fourth photographs. SEE ALSO BOTANICAL_QUESTIONS entry 20, which flags a factual error in this species' published teaser (sign copy), and entry 19 — this plant is the on-site reference for the rare fruit bridge comparison.
